title: Rain and dew prayers
hookLine: on Shemini Atzeret and Passover the seasonal prayer switches between rain and dew

cards: Someone in rainy London and someone in dry Phoenix open the same prayer book in the autumn. And on the same day, both start praying for rain. Not for their own city.
For a small strip of land on the eastern Mediterranean, where the rains come between autumn and spring, and where, in ancient times, whether they came decided whether people ate.
Twice a year, the Amidah changes one line, to follow the seasons of a land some of them have never seen.

teach.b: In the second blessing of the Amidah, the one about God's power, there's a seasonal line. In winter: mashiv haruach umorid hageshem, who makes the wind blow and the rain fall. Geshem means rain.
The switch happens at Musaf on Shemini Atzeret, the day after Sukkot, just as the rainy season in the Land of Israel begins.
The cantor, often dressed in white as on the High Holy Days, chants a special prayer for rain, Tefillat Geshem.
Its medieval poem remembers the ancestors and water. Abraham, who followed God like flowing water. Isaac, whose servants dug wells.
Jacob, who rolled the stone from the well. Moses, drawn from the water. And the tribes, who crossed the sea.

teach.h: ON PASSOVER, THE PRAYER FOR DEW.
teach.b: Then, on the first day of Passover, as the rains end, the cantor chants a prayer for dew, Tefillat Tal.
After that, many communities, especially in Israel and among Sephardim, say morid hatal, who makes the dew fall, all summer. Others say nothing until autumn.
Why is rain in a blessing about God's power?

The Talmud says there are three keys God keeps and gives to no messenger: the key of rain, the key of birth, and the key of bringing the dead to life. Rain sits in the same blessing as the hope of life restored.
Dry seed, buried, comes up green. And dew? The rabbis taught that dew is never held back.
It comes quietly, night after night, even when nothing else falls. Rain is a request. Dew is a gift that's always there.

how: Tefillat Geshem is chanted in Musaf on Shemini Atzeret, after which 'who makes the wind blow and the rain fall' is added to the Amidah until Passover; Tefillat Tal is chanted on the first day of Passover, after which many communities say 'who makes the dew fall' through the summer.

o: the wind that comes before the autumn storms
the dew prayed for on the first day of Passover
rain, praised in the Amidah through the winter

games.q: rain and dew — tap the pairs.

s: Jews pray for rain according to their own local climate
the prayer follows the seasons of the Land of Israel.
the Talmud calls rain a key God gives to no messenger
with the keys of birth and of reviving the dead.
every community says a line for dew all summer
many do, especially in Israel and among Sephardim; others say nothing.

games.q: you live somewhere rainy all year. it's Shemini Atzeret. what does your prayer book ask for now?
o: rain, for the Land of Israel's season.
games.why: from Shemini Atzeret, the Amidah praises the one who makes the rain fall, following the Land of Israel's rains.

practice: Look outside, or picture the sky over you today, wet or dry, warm or cold, and then the soil under the nearest tree and what the season is doing to it.
If you pray, give thanks for rain, or for dew, whichever the season brings; if not, simply thank the weather for keeping things alive.

wordCard.voice: Geshem. Rain. The prayer chanted on Shemini Atzeret, when the Amidah begins to praise the one who makes the rain fall.

orig.note: Hebrew: rain, as in morid hageshem, who makes the rain fall.

carryVoice: Your line: rain and dew. Two seasons, one line in the Amidah. Day six hundred thirty-one, done.
